title: Mechanisms of Prompt-Induced Hallucination in Vision-Language Models
text: The University of Texas at Austin, 2 Brown University, 3 Technion, 4 University of Tübingen, 5 Harvard University {michal_golovanevsky, william_rudman}@brown.edu Vision–language models (VLMs) often follow textual prompts even when they contradict visual evidence Deng et al. ( 2025 ); Zhang et al. ( 2025 ); Hua et al. ( 2025 ) . These hallucinations are a growing concern as VLMs are deployed in real-world settings with noisy or inaccurate user inputs. To better understand this behavior, we study prompt-induced hallucinations (PIH) in a controlled object-counting setting, where prompts systematically overestimate the number of objects in an image. Figure 1 illustrates the phenomenon where, although the model correctly counts three waterlilies when asked directly, it hallucinates additional, nonexistent flowers when asked to describe a mismatched count (e.g., “Describe the four waterlilies”). This undesirable behavior is unlikely to be driven by limitations in numerical reasoning Zhang et al. ( 2023a ); Rahmanzadehgervi et al. ( 2024 ); Rudman et al. ( 2025 ) , since the model correctly solves the underlying counting task. Instead, this is consistent with a known tendency of VLMs to rely on textual prompts over conflicting visual evidence Deng et al. ( 2025 ) . To characterize PIH, we study when such errors occur and how they can be reduced via targeted analysis of attention-heads. Across models, PIH outputs follow a consistent and structured pattern.
